The foundational structure of integration theory hinges upon the extension of classical Riemann integration into a more robust framework—Lebesgue integration—which allows for broader classes of functions to be integrated. This is achieved by defining integrability in terms of measurable sets and functions, thereby enabling the treatment of functions that may not be Riemann integrable. The concept of extended integration further broadens applicability by permitting functions whose positive and negative parts are not both finite, thus allowing for integrals that evaluate to ±∞. In the context of GSE, these primitives support dynamic systems modeling through measurable transitions and state updates. For GSI, they provide the theoretical basis for probabilistic inference, particularly in handling complex likelihoods and posteriors over measurable event spaces. The Lebesgue-Stieltjes integral extends this to include weighted integrals with respect to arbitrary increasing functions, offering flexibility in modeling cumulative effects and transformations. The series convergence criterion provides a discrete analog, useful for numerical approximations and discrete-event simulations. Each primitive exhibits a dual nature: mathematically precise yet operationally flexible, supporting both theoretical rigor and computational tractability.
